4058 AF4E 0450  20 	b *r0
4059               	;
4060               	; 	' THE FONT'S COLOUR TABLE WAS 472 BYTES OF ONE REPEATED VALUE, which is a
4061               	; 	' fifth of what the fixed area had left. DEFINE COLOR copies such a table
4062               	; 	' out of ROM into all three screen thirds; writing the constant straight
4063               	; 	' into the colour table does the same job for the price of a loop, and
4064               	; 	' the loop runs once, at boot.
4065               	; 	'
4066               	; 	' The colour table is at >2000 and the VDP mirrors it once per screen
4067               	; 	' third, >800 apart. Both numbers were read out of the GENERATED assembly
4068               	; 	' -- define_color's `ai r0,>2000` and LDIRVM3's `ai r0,>0800` -- rather
4069               	; 	' than assumed, because a wrong base here would paint over the pattern
4070               	; 	' table and the failure would look like corrupt artwork.
4071               	; 	'
4072               	; 	' Paced: a few hundred VDP writes in one frame are silently dropped.
4073               	; 	' THE SCANNER'S COLOURS ARE THREE BLOCKS REPEATED SIXTEEN TIMES EACH, so
4074               	; 	' the table shipped 384 bytes to say 24 bytes' worth. Same trick as the
4075               	; 	' font: write the colour table directly. >2000 is the colour table's base
4076               	; 	' and >800 the stride between screen thirds -- the same layout DEFINE COLOR
4077               	; 	' walks for us in setup_font, which this cannot use because it is cheaper to
4078               	; 	' expand 24 bytes here than to ship 384 in the bank.
4079               	; 	' NOTHING IS UNDER THE GROUND FLOOR, SO NOTHING SHOULD BE GREEN THERE.
4080               	; 	' A floor bar is five pixels of yellow over three of the green air
4081               	; 	' belonging to the floor BELOW it (see SLAB), which is right for three of
4082               	; 	' the four bars and wrong for the last one: below floor 0 there is no
4083               	; 	' floor, only the scanner, and the green read as a strip of shop with
4084               	; 	' nothing in it.
4085               	; 	'
4086               	; 	' NO NEW CHARACTER IS NEEDED, BECAUSE THE COLOUR TABLE HAS THREE COPIES
4087               	; 	' -- one per eight screen rows -- and the bands land such that each bar
4088               	; 	' sits in a different third:
4089               	; 	'
4090               	; 	'     band 0 roof   rows  1-5    bar row  5   third 0
4091               	; 	'     band 1        rows  6-10   bar row 10   third 1
4092               	; 	'     band 2        rows 11-15   bar row 15   third 1
4093               	; 	'     band 3 GROUND rows 16-20   bar row 20   third 2
4094               	; 	'
4095               	; 	' so recolouring SLAB in third 2 alone reaches the ground floor's bar and
4096               	; 	' nothing else. The same third also holds the scanner, but the scanner
4097               	; 	' does not use these characters. This is the same mechanism that once hid
4098               	; 	' a bug for months (CLAUDE.md 3A, the blanked-in-one-third note) used
4099               	; 	' deliberately for once.
4100               	; 	'
4101               	; 	' Only the three bottom lines change, and only their BACKGROUND: SLAB has
4102               	; 	' no ink there and SLABE's brick keeps its grey.
4103               	; floor0_colour:
4104               cvb_FLOOR0_COLOUR
4105               	; 	' TWO CHARACTERS, THE SAME THREE SCAN LINES, ONE ROUTINE. Both blocks
4106               	; 	' were written out in full and differed only in which character and which
4107               	; 	' colour byte -- eleven statements twice, including the multiply-by-eight
4108               	; 	' done by doubling (`*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, which clobbers r0,
4109               	; 	' CLAUDE.md 3A).
4110               	; 	f0c = CH_SLAB

4324               	;
4325               	; 	' ======================================================================
4326               	; 	' TITLE
4327               	; 	' ======================================================================
4328               	; 	' DRAWING THE TITLE AND WAITING ON IT ARE TWO ROUTINES, because the boot
4329               	; 	' does something between them: the rest of setup runs while this is on
4330               	; 	' screen. They used to be one, which is why the title could not be shown
4331               	; 	' until everything was ready.
4332               	; 	' THE TITLE IS A DISPLAY LIST IN A ROM BANK, not twelve PRINT ATs.
4333               	; 	'
4334               	; 	' CVBasic embeds a string literal in the FIXED AREA, which is the only
4335               	; 	' budget that cannot be grown -- linkticart writes exactly three loader
4336               	; 	' pages and discards the rest, and they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
4337               	; 	' >A000 rather than cart ROM. 190 characters of title text were sitting
4338               	; 	' in the scarcest place in the program.
4339               	; 	'
4340               	; 	' AND THE REAL POINT IS WHAT IT COSTS NEXT TIME. With the text in a
4341               	; 	' table, changing what the title says or where it sits is an edit to
4342               	; 	' assets/gentitle.py and a rebuild. It costs bank bytes, of which there
4343               	; 	' are thousands, instead of fixed-area bytes, of which there are tens.
4344               	; 	'
4345               	; 	' The table is `row, col, length, bytes...` with 255 to end. ROW AND
4346               	; 	' COLUMN rather than a 16-bit screen offset, because reassembling one
4347               	; 	' from two bytes needs a multiply, and on the TMS9900 MPY clobbers r0 --
4348               	; 	' the next line that reads the product's variable gets the HIGH word
4349               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). Five doublings have no such hazard and are smaller.
4350               	; title_draw:
4351               cvb_TITLE_DRAW
4352               	; 	#if NES
4353               	; 	' THE TITLE SITS ON DARK BLUE, AND THE BACKDROP IS THE ONLY WAY TO SAY SO.
4354               	; 	'
4355               	; 	' Palette index 0 is the UNIVERSAL backdrop -- every background palette's
4356               	; 	' entry 0 is the same colour, so it cannot be set per region the way the
4357               	; 	' sky and the store are. It was never written at all, which is why every
4358               	; 	' cell that maps to index 0 came out black, the title page included.
4359               	; 	'
4360               	; 	' Writing it here and putting it back in draw_screen costs two statements

4533               	;
4534               	; 	' NO ALPHA LOCK CALIBRATION, AND THERE USED TO BE ONE.
4535               	; 	'
4536               	; 	' The premise was that ALPHA LOCK shares a line with the joystick's
4537               	; 	' VERTICAL axis, so a latched key reports a direction that is never
4538               	; 	' released -- fatal here, where down is the duck and up is the lift. The
4539               	; 	' guard sampled the axis for forty frames before listening and then
4540               	; 	' ignored any direction that had been held for essentially all of them.
4541               	; 	'
4542               	; 	' IT WAS REMOVED BECAUSE THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD UP.
4543               	; 	'
4544               	; 	'   * CLAUDE.md claimed every other game here dodged the problem by not
4545               	; 	'     reading up/down. EIGHT of them do read it -- Adventire, Astiroids,
4546               	; 	'     HardHatMack, Ms. Pac-Man, RallyX, Structris, UFO, Bust-A-Bobble --
4547               	; 	'     and not one has a calibration or has ever shown the fault.
4548               	; 	'   * It never fired on the machine this is developed on: the notice it
4549               	; 	'     prints when it detects a stuck axis has never appeared.
4550               	; 	'   * The original evidence was that the game "came up and would not
4551               	; 	'     start" -- and the first version BLOCKED until the axis cleared. That
4552               	; 	'     symptom is indistinguishable from the several input bugs since found
4553               	; 	'     and fixed for real: keys arriving at a screen that was not listening
4554               	; 	'     yet. The diagnosis was probably one of those.
4555               	; 	'
4556               	; 	' It also cost two bugs of its own: forty frames of a drawn but deaf title
4557               	; 	' screen, which swallowed the first digit of 8-3-8, and a wrong theory
4558               	; 	' about keyboard noise that led to a filter which ate real presses.
4559               	; 	'
4560               	; 	' If a stuck axis ever does appear it will be obvious -- the player will
4561               	; 	' duck or ride the lift without asking -- and the guard is in the history.
4562               	;
4563               	; title_input:

4569               	; 	' title_draw runs early on purpose (DESIGN.md 0d-nonies) so the screen
4570               	; 	' arrives instead of filling in, but setup_rest, init_tables and the

4572               	; 	' finished, and completely deaf. A player types 8-3-8 into that window and

4607               	; 	' THE MARQUEE CHASES WHILE THE TITLE WAITS.
4608               	; 	'
4609               	; 	' ONLY TWO CHARACTERS CHANGE PER STEP. At any moment exactly one of the
4610               	; 	' four lamps is blank; a step lights the one that was blank and blanks the
4611               	; 	' next one round. Redefining all four would be twice the work for the same
4612               	; 	' picture.
4613               	; 	'
4614               	; 	' IT IS BELOW THE INPUT READS, deliberately. This loop's history is input
4615               	; 	' bugs -- a screen that was drawn but not listening, a keypress eaten by a
4616               	; 	' stability filter -- so nothing that is merely decoration goes in front of
4617               	; 	' the polling. A dropped frame of animation is invisible; a dropped
4618               	; 	' keypress is what took three sessions to find.
4619               	; 	' `bphs` IS WHICH LAMP IS DARK, and a step is: light that one, move on,
4620               	; 	' darken the next. The character number is arithmetic rather than a
4621               	; 	' four-way branch -- DEFINE CHAR takes an expression, so the whole chase
4622               	; 	' is two calls and no `IF` ladder. The ladder version was eight DEFINE
4623               	; 	' CHARs across four branches and cost about three hundred bytes for the
4624               	; 	' same picture.
4625               	; 	'
4626               	; 	' TWO CALLS, NOT FIVE. Lighting all four and then darkening one is the
4627               	; 	' same result and reads more simply, but two separate DEFINEs can have a
4628               	; 	' vblank between them, so the sign would show ALL lamps lit for a frame
4629               	; 	' every step -- a flash rather than a chase. Only ever changing the two
4630               	; 	' lamps that actually change cannot do that.
4631               	; 	bfr = bfr - 1

4649               	; 		' QUEUED, NOT BLANKED -- AND THIS IS WHAT MADE THE TITLE FLASH.
4650               	; 		'
4651               	; 		' nes_def turns rendering OFF and waits for a vblank the NMI
4652               	; 		' therefore never services, so the game's own WAIT then waits for
4653               	; 		' the one after: about two frames with the picture switched off.
4654               	; 		' Twice a marquee step, for ever, on the one screen the player
4655               	; 		' looks at longest. It reads as the whole title flashing, not as
4656               	; 		' the bulbs animating.

4659               	; 		' turned off and no frame is lost -- and both bulbs land in the

4695               	; 		#if NES
4696               	; 		' A SECOND STAGING AREA, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE MARQUEE BUG.
4697               	; 		'
4698               	; 		' nes_escd does NOT copy anything. It builds the tile into the RAM
4699               	; 		' buffer `#nesb` and hands the NMI a five-byte descriptor holding a
4700               	; 		' POINTER to it; the copy happens at the next vblank. Both marquee
4701               	; 		' writes happen in the same pass, so with one buffer the darken call
4702               	; 		' overwrote the staged LIT bytes before the NMI had read either --
4703               	; 		' and then BOTH descriptors copied bulb_off.
4704               	; 		'
4705               	; 		' So every step darkened two lamps and lit none, and the sign walked
4706               	; 		' itself out: "it animates a little bit and goes out". Nothing fails,
4707               	; 		' because both writes are perfectly valid and land exactly where they
4708               	; 		' were addressed -- they just carry the same sixteen bytes.
4709               	; 		'
4710               	; 		' The lit call staged at nesb(0); this one stages sixteen bytes up.
4711               	; 		' nesb is 96 bytes for the escalator's six characters and the
4712               	; 		' escalator never runs on the title screen, so the room is free. The
4713               	; 		' pointer is put back immediately: esc_tick stages at offset 0 and
4714               	; 		' would otherwise write its six characters one tile off.
4715               	; 		#nesb = #nesb + 16
4716               	; 		#nsrc = VARPTR bulb_off(0)
4717               	; 		nchr = bcode
4718               	; 		ncnt = 1
4719               	; 		ntab = 1
4720               	; 		#ncol = 0
4721               	; 		nink = 3
4722               	; 		GOSUB nes_escd			' queued -- see the note above
4723               	; 		#nesb = #nesb - 16
4724               	; 		#else
4725               	; 		DEFINE CHAR bcode,1,bulb_off
4726 B2C4 0980  32 	srl r0,8
4727 B2C6 C100  18 	mov r0,r4

4845               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).

4847               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
4848               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
4849               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
4850               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
4851               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
4852               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
4853               	; 	'
4854               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
4855               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
4856               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
4857               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
4858               	; 	'
4859               	; 	' The reset is the DEFAULT rather than a test for a particular wrong digit:
4860               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.

5309               	; 	' From the lift on screen 3 that is 5,120 px against the 4,208 he walked

5586               	;
5587               	; 	' ======================================================================
5588               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5589               	; 	' ======================================================================
5590               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5591               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5592               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5593               	; 	' of running.
5594               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5595               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5596               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5597               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5598               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5599               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5600               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5601               	; 	'
5602               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5603               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5604               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5605               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5606               	; 	'
5607               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5608               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5609               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5610               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5611               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5612               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5613               	; 	'
5614               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5615               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5616               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5617               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5618               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5619               	; 	'
5620               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5621               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends

5696               	; 		#ddst = #ddst + 96		' three rows down -- see the overscan note
5697               	; 		' ONE ROW A FRAME, AND THIS IS WHY THREE BANDS IN FOUR LOST THEIR
5698               	; 		' LAST TWO ROWS. The NMI copies PPUBUF into the PPU during vblank
5699               	; 		' and its copy loop DOES NOT STOP WHEN VBLANK ENDS -- it runs to
5700               	; 		' the end of the descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and a
5701               	; 		' PPUDATA write outside vblank is discarded by the hardware.
5702               	; 		'
5703               	; 		' NTSC gives about 2273 CPU cycles of vblank, OAM DMA takes 513 of
5704               	; 		' them, and the copy costs roughly 14 a byte: about a hundred bytes
5705               	; 		' get through. A 32x5 band is 160, so the last sixty-odd vanished
5706               	; 		' -- three whole rows arrived, the fourth stopped eight or nine
5707               	; 		' cells in, and the floor bar and the air row above it were simply
5708               	; 		' never there. Measured on screen as `#########.......`, on every
5709               	; 		' band whose blit did not happen to start early.
5710               	; 		'

5771               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5772               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5773               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5774               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5775               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5776               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5777               	; 	'
5778               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5779               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5780               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5781               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5782               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5783               	; 	'
5784               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5785               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5786               	; 	' above it at all.
5787               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5788               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green
5789               	; 	' under it: a beam there already ran straight into grey and needed
5790               	; 	' nothing. Giving the roof its three green rows (so the lift shaft stops
5791               	; 	' under it, like every other floor) took that away, and the top floor's
5792               	; 	' beams started falling three pixels short.
5793               	; 	'
5794               	; 	' So the roof gets its own version of the stamp. A beam HOLDS THE ROOF
5795               	; 	' UP and must reach it; the shaft merely stops beneath it.

6412               	; 			' PER KIND, not one global speed (see start_krook).
6413               	; 			' THE SPEED IS A PROPERTY OF THE KIND, and obs() only ever
6414               	; 			' held a copy of it -- set from the kind here, zeroed for a
6415               	; 			' radio below, and read in one place. upd_obst derives it
6416               	; 			' from obk() instead, which is 8 bytes of RAM back and one
6417               	; 			' fewer thing that can disagree with itself.
6418               	; 			' THEY COME FROM THE FAR SIDE. Kelly walked into this screen
6419               	; 			' from one edge, so the obstacles start at the OTHER edge and
6420               	; 			' run toward him. Crossing a seam then always presents an
6421               	; 			' ONCOMING stream, never a set of backs he has to catch up
6422               	; 			' with -- and it means the direction he is travelling is
6423               	; 			' always the direction the danger comes from.
6424               	; 			'
6425               	; 			' The table's x becomes a stagger from that edge rather than
6426               	; 			' an absolute position, and the slot index spreads them out
6427               	; 			' so they arrive in sequence instead of as one wall.
6428               	; 			'
6429               	; 			' THE SECOND ONE IS A FIXED DISTANCE BEHIND THE FIRST, AND
6430               	; 			' THAT DISTANCE IS SET BY THE JUMP.
6431               	; 			'
6432               	; 			' It used to be `(lx AND 63) + 64` -- a masked byte out of
6433               	; 			' the placement table plus a constant -- so the gap between
6434               	; 			' the two hazards was whatever those two bytes happened to
6435               	; 			' differ by. Measured across the five populated screens it
6436               	; 			' came out 46, 46, 70, 70, 70 px. Screens 2 and 4 flank the
6437               	; 			' elevator, so the store had a visibly tighter pair on one
6438               	; 			' side of it than the other, which is exactly how it was
6439               	; 			' reported from play.
6440               	; 			'
6441               	; 			' Both numbers are too small, which is the real fault. Kelly
6442               	; 			' closes on an oncoming hazard at (KWALK64 + its speed)/64
6443               	; 			' px a FRAME, and the jump is airborne 28 frames, so a jump
6444               	; 			' eats 82 px of closing distance at the fastest hazard. At
6445               	; 			' 46 or 70 there is NO screen where he can land between the
6446               	; 			' two: he clears the first and comes down on the second.
6447               	; 			'
6448               	; 			' HAZGAP is that distance with margin, and it agrees with
6449               	; 			' the original to within 4 px (see the CONST). The pairing
6450               	; 			' is now a fact about the jump rather than an accident of
6451               	; 			' two bytes. assets/checkspace.py measures it and fails the
6452               	; 			' build.
6453               	; 			' THE SECOND SLOT IS MEASURED FROM THE FIRST, not from its
6454               	; 			' own table byte. Adding HAZGAP to its own `lx AND 63` would
6455               	; 			' still leave the GAP varying by up to 63 px between screens
6456               	; 			' -- the same fault in a politer form, and the reason the two
6457               	; 			' sides of the elevator differed in the first place. Holding
6458               	; 			' slot 0's stagger and adding to that makes the gap exactly
6459               	; 			' HAZGAP on every screen, while slot 0 still lands wherever
6460               	; 			' the table puts it, so the placement variety is untouched.
6461               	; 			' DERIVED FROM THE BAND, not stored. The table used to carry
6462               	; 			' an x byte per slot; slot 1's was ignored outright (it is
6463               	; 			' `stg0 + HAZGAP`) and slot 0's only reached the game as its
6464               	; 			' low six bits. `lix` is the band index, already in hand,

6562               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6563               	; 			'
6564               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6565               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6566               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6567               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6568               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6569               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6570               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6571               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6572               	; 			'
6573               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6574               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6575               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6576               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6577               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6578               	; 			'
6579               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6580               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6581               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6582               	; 			'
6583               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6584               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6585               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6586               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6587               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
6588               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.
6589               	; 			' obp is a BALL-only field: upd_obst reads it under an
6590               	; 			' IF uk = OB_BALL and nothing else touches it, and every
6591               	; 			' ball has it computed below. It was seeded here from a
6592               	; 			' table byte that no longer exists, and for anything but
6593               	; 			' a ball that seed was never read.
6594               	; 			IF lk = OB_BALL THEN

7568               	; 		' HE IS STANDING ON A STEP, so he moves at the STEP's rate: 2 px
7569               	; 		' across and 1 up PER PASS -- the staircase's own slope, and exactly
7570               	; 		' what one phase of esc_tick moves the pattern by.
7571               	; 		'
7572               	; 		' NOT `fdv`, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. Everything else in this loop
7573               	; 		' is paced by the frame delta, and pacing him that way too made him
7574               	; 		' outrun the steps the moment a pass cost more than one frame: his
7575               	; 		' feet started planted on a tread and ended floating above it.

7579               	; 		' is the one where both are driven by the same fixed step, so the
7580               	; 		' rider is clocked by the pass, like the steps he is standing on.

8121               	; 		' THE FIRST STEP OFF THE MARK IS ALWAYS HEARD. sfw is a distance --
8122               	; 		' a step every fifteen pixels -- so a short tap of the stick moved
8123               	; 		' him a few pixels and made NO sound at all. That does not read as
8124               	; 		' a short step, it reads as the controls being ignored, and it is
8125               	; 		' worst exactly where a player taps rather than holds: lining up a
8126               	; 		' jump, or edging around a hazard.
8127               	; 		'
8128               	; 		' Priming the accumulator to the threshold makes the very next pass
8129               	; 		' fire. It does not cheat the RATE: the trigger subtracts fifteen
8130               	; 		' rather than zeroing, so the pixels actually travelled still carry
8131               	; 		' into the following step and a held run comes out at 6.9 a second

9059               	;
9060               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
9061               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
9062               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
9063               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
9064               	; 	'
9065               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
9066               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
9067               	; 	'
9068               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
9069               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
9070               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
9071               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
9072               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
9073               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
9074               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
9075               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
9076               	; 	' merged object.
9077               	; 	'
9078               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
9079               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
9080               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
9081               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
9082               	; 	'
9083               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
9084               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
9085               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
9086               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
9087               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
9088               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
9089               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
9090               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
9091               	; 	'
9092               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
9093               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
9094               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
9095               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
9096               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
9097               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
9098               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
9099               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
9100               	; 	' its bottom half together.
9101               	; 	'
9102               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
9103               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
9104               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
9105               	; 	#if NES
9106               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
9107               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
9108               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
9109               	; 	'
9110               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
9111               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
9112               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
9113               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
9114               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
9115               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
9116               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
9117               	; 	'
9118               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
9119               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
9120               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
9121               	; 	'
9122               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
9123               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
9124               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
9125               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
9126               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
9127               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
9128               	; 	'                   the whole time.
9129               	; 	'
9130               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
9131               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
9132               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
9133               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
9134               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
9135               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
9136               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
9137               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
9138               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
9139               	; 	'
9140               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
9141               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
9142               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
9143               	; 	' they only need setting once.
9144               	; 	'
9145               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
9146               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
9147               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
9148               	; 	' as him changing pose.
9149               	; nes_swp16:
9150               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
9151               	; 	'
9152               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
9153               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
9154               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
9155               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
9156               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
9157               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
9158               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
9159               	; 	'
9160               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
9161               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
9162               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
9163               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
9164               	; 	'
9165               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
9166               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
9167               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
9168               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
9169               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
9170               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
9171               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
9172               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
9173               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
9174               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2
9175               	; 	nchr = P_HSTB
9176               	; 	ntab = 0
9177               	; 	#ncol = 0
9178               	; 	nink = 1
9179               	; 	ncnt = 4
9180               	; 	WAIT
9181               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9182               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32		' four patterns of source art, 8 bytes each
9183               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9184               	; 	WAIT
9185               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9186               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
9187               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9188               	; 	WAIT
9189               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9190               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
9191               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9192               	; 	WAIT
9193               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9194               	; 	RETURN
9195               	;
9196               	; nes_def:
9197               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
9198               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
9199               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
9200               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
9201               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
9202               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
9203               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
9204               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
9205               	; 	RETURN
9206               	;
9207               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
9208               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
9209               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
9210               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
9211               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
9212               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
9213               	; 	'
9214               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
9215               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
9216               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
9217               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
9218               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
9219               	; 	' flashing title screen.
9220               	; 	'
9221               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
9222               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
9223               	; nes_escd:
9224               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrq
9225               	; 	RETURN
9226               	;

10013               	; 	' THE BOUNCE PHASE, ON THE SAME CLOCK AS THE JUMP AND AT ITS OLD PERIOD.
10014               	; 	'
10015               	; 	' The jump has always advanced by the frame delta (`kjf = kjf + fdv`) while
10016               	; 	' the bounce advanced once per PASS -- so whether a jump cleared a ball
10017               	; 	' depended on how busy the screen was, and the frame-by-frame property
10018               	; 	' checkball.py proves was exact only at fdv = 1.
10019               	; 	'
10020               	; 	' Stepping the phase by fdv directly would fix the clock and wreck the
10021               	; 	' game: a 32-phase arc would drop from about 1.35 s to 0.55 s, balls
10022               	; 	' bouncing 2.4x faster everywhere. So it gets a fraction of its own --
10023               	; 	' 25/64 of a phase per frame is 23.4 phases a second, against the 23.8 it
10024               	; 	' runs at today. Same bounce, now the same clock as the thing that has to
10025               	; 	' clear it.

10271               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10272               	; 	'
10273               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10274               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10275               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10276               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10277               	; 	'
10278               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10279               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10280               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10281               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10282               	; 	'
10283               	; 	' TWO DRAINS CAP THE STEP AT 2 PER FRAME whatever psp64 says (CLAUDE.md
10284               	; 	' 3A: N drains cap the speed at N, and the surplus leaks into a byte that
10285               	; 	' wraps). Every caller is under that: Kelly 102/64 = 1.6, the fastest
10286               	; 	' hazard 76/64 = 1.2, Harry 57/64 = 0.9, the bounce phase 25/64 = 0.4.
10287               	; 	'
10288               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10289               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10290               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10291               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10292               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10293               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.

10782               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10783               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10784               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10785               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10786               	; 	' runs every pass.
10787               	; 	'
10788               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10789               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10790               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10791               	; 	'
10792               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10793               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10794               	; 	'
10795               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10796               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10797               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10798               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10799               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10800               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10801               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10802               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10803               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10804               	; 	'
10805               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10806               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10807               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10808               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10809               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10810               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
10811               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
10812               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,
10813               	; 	' not after it. It sat below the two `IF hmv` blocks, where all it could
10814               	; 	' still reach was the animation counter: he faced the right way, played
10815               	; 	' the run cycle and did not travel a pixel. He stood at the foot of the

10913               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10914               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10915               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10916               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10917               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10918               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10919               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10920               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10921               	; 	'
10922               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10923               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10924               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10925               	; 	'
10926               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10927               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10928               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10929               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10930               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10931               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10932               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10933               	; 	'
10934               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10935               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10936               	; 	'
10937               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10938               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10939               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10940               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10941               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10942               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10943               	; 	'
10944               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10945               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10946               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10947               	; 	' before any of this.
10948               	; 	'
10949               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10950               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10951               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10952               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10953               	; 	' journey.
10954               	; 	'
10955               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
10956               	; 	' travelled, not time -- so the run cycle stays locked to the ground at any
10957               	; 	' rate. A 9 px step moves it exactly one pose of its 8 px beat.
10958               	; 	pacc = hacc

10992               	; 			' constant the escape target uses, so the place he stops
10993               	; 			' and the place he escapes from cannot disagree.
10994               	; 			' MEASURE THE ROOM, THEN STEP -- and never add past the
10995               	; 			' limit, so this is exact for ANY limit up to 255.
10996               	; 			'
10997               	; 			' The obvious `hx = hx + hspd : IF hx > hlim THEN hx = hlim`
10998               	; 			' is a byte or two cheaper and quietly caps XROOF at 245.
10999               	; 			' `pace_step` can emit two pixels a frame over five frames,
11000               	; 			' so hspd reaches 10; at hlim 252 the sum is 262, which in
11001               	; 			' eight bits is 6, and `IF 6 > 252` is false -- the crook
11002               	; 			' would TELEPORT TO THE WEST WALL on his last stride. Only
11003               	; 			' at a speed nobody has set yet, which is the worst kind.

11418               	;
11419               	; 	' ======================================================================
11420               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11421               	; 	' ======================================================================
11422               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11423               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11424               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11425               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11426               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11427               	; 	'
11428               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11429               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11430               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11431               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11432               	; 	' broken.
11433               	; 	'
11434               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11435               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11436               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11437               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11438               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11439               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11440               	; 	'
11441               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11442               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11443               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11444               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11445               	; coll_obst:
11446               cvb_COLL_OBST

11818               	; 	'

12001               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
12002               	; 	'
12003               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
12004               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
12005               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
12006               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
12007               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
12008               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
12009               	; 	'
12010               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
12011               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
12012               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.
12013               	; 	'
12014               	; 	' UNSIGNED-SAFE. Riding up is above the shared floor and riding down is
12015               	; 	' below it, which is a signed quantity, and CVBasic's variables are not.
12016               	; 	' So both are collected as POSITIVE heights on opposite sides -- Kelly's
12017               	; 	' climb plus Harry's descent on one side, Harry's climb on the other --
12018               	; 	' and the difference is taken between two numbers that cannot go
12019               	; 	' negative. Two riders passing on the same flight measure the sum of
12020               	; 	' their heights, which is exactly the distance between them.

13264               	; 	' ======================================================================
13265               	; 	' THE SCANNER
13266               	; 	' ======================================================================
13267               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
13268               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
13269               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
13270               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
13271               	; 	'
13272               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
13273               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
13274               	; 	'
13275               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
13276               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
13277               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
13278               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
13279               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
13280               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
13281               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
13282               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
13283               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
13284               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
13285               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.
13286               	; esc_tick:
13287               cvb_ESC_TICK
13288               	; 	' ONLY SCREENS 0 AND 7 CARRY A FLIGHT, so six screens in eight skip this
13289               	; 	' entirely -- which is what makes rewriting the cells every frame
13290               	; 	' affordable. Nested, not `klsc > 0 AND klsc < 7`: the 9900 backend
13291               	; 	' miscompiles a compare-AND-compare (CLAUDE.md 3A).
13292               	; 	IF klsc > 0 THEN

13311               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
13312               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13313               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13314               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13315               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13316               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13317               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13318               	; 	'
13319               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
13320               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13321               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13322               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13323               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13324               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13325               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.
13326               	; 	escp = escp + 1

13339               	; 	#if NES
13340               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13341               	; 	'
13342               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13343               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13344               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13345               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13346               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13347               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13348               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13349               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13350               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13351               	; 	'
13352               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13353               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13354               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13355               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13356               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13357               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13358               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13359               	; 	'
13360               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13361               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13362               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13363               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13364               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13365               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13366               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13367               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13368               	; 	' with room to spare.
13369               	; 	'
13370               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13371               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13372               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13373               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13374               	; 	WAIT
13375               	; 	#endif
13376               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13377               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13378               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13379               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13380               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13381               	; 	'
13382               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13383               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13384               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13385               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13386               	; 	'
13387               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
13388               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
13389               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
13390               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
13391               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are
13392               	; 	' PIXEL-IDENTICAL and are never wanted in the same screen THIRD, so they
13393               	; 	' share their characters now and are told apart by the per-third colour
13394               	; 	' table (see esc_deck_col in setup). Six either side.
13395               	; 	'
13396               	; 	' The handrail and the frame sit past the end of both ranges and never
13397               	; 	' move at all.

13725               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
13726               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is
13727               	; 	' somewhere, but not what he is near, which is the one thing you actually
13728               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say
13729               	; 	' where that floor's escalator is, and the bar says where the elevator is --
13730               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
13731               	; 	'
13732               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level
13733               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries
13734               	; 	' exactly one colour here:
13735               	; 	'
13736               	; 	'   +0  GREY    escalator head, and the elevator car
13737               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
13738               	; 	'   +2  GREY
13739               	; 	'   +3  YELLOW  the floor line -- and NOTHING else goes here
13740               	; 	'
13741               	; 	' THE FIRST THREE ROWS ARE THE FLOOR'S AIR AND EVERYTHING LIVES IN THEM:
13742               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all
13743               	; 	' three pixels tall. They are grey in the table, and the Kop and the
13744               	; 	' crook recolour their own CHARACTER as they move (scan_mark) -- which is
13745               	; 	' what lets both of them fill the band instead of getting a pixel row
13746               	; 	' each. Eight pixels of this canvas is half a screen of the store, so
13747               	; 	' they are almost never in one character; when they are, they merge.
13748               	; 	'
13749               	; 	' Shrinking from six rows bought eight empty pixel rows, four above the
13750               	; 	' instrument and four below, so it no longer butts against the shop floor
13751               	; 	' above it or the bottom of the screen.

14024               	; 	' A LEVEL BAND IS SIX PIXEL ROWS ON THE NES AND FOUR ON THE TI.
14025               	; 	'
14026               	; 	' It was six everywhere once. It shrank to four to buy eight empty pixel
14027               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did
14028               	; 	' not butt against the shop floor above it and the bottom of the screen.
14029               	; 	'

14031               	; 	' thirty rows to the TI's twenty-four, so the strip runs past the canvas to
14032               	; 	' the bottom edge and the grey either side of the instrument is real cells
14033               	; 	' rather than blank rows inside it. That gives the band its two rows back,
14034               	; 	' and the instrument goes from 16 pixels tall to 24 -- half again, which is
14035               	; 	' what "not quite so vertically thin" asks for.

14188               	;
14189               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
14190               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
14191               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
14192               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
14193               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
14194               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
14195               	; scan_wipe:
14196               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
14197               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
14198               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
14199               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
14200               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
14201               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
14202               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
14203               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
14204               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
14205               	; 	'
14206               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
14207               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
14208               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
14209               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
14210               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
14211               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
14212               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
14213               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
14214               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
14215               	; 	'
14216               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
14217               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
14218               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
14219               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
14220               	; 	'
14221               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
14222               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.
14223               	; 	#swa = 5760			' 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8, the canvas patterns

14226               	; 	#if NES
14227               	; 	' AN NES TILE IS SIXTEEN BYTES, NOT EIGHT -- two bitplanes. DERIVED FROM
14228               	; 	' THE LINE ABOVE rather than written out again: renumber.py rewrites that
14229               	; 	' literal out of genart.SCAN_FIRST and checkstruct.py checks it, and a
14230               	; 	' second hand-kept copy of the same number is exactly the fault recorded
14231               	; 	' in the comment above this routine.
14232               	; 	#swa = #swa + #swa
14233               	; 	#swa = #swa - 4096
14234               	; 	#endif
14235               	; 	' THE SHADOW TAKES ITS BASE FROM THE LINE ABOVE, never from a second
14236               	; 	' copy of the number. renumber.py rewrites that literal out of
14237               	; 	' genart.SCAN_FIRST, and a hand-kept duplicate of it is precisely the
14238               	; 	' fault recorded in the comment above -- one copy moved, the other did
14239               	; 	' not, and the wipe spent months clearing the wrong forty-eight
14240               	; 	' characters. 6 x 64 is 384, which is the size of nsc.
14241               	; 	#if NES
14242               	; 	#nsb = #swa
14243               	; 	#nsi = 0
14244               	; 	#endif
14245               	; 	#if NES
14246               	; 	' TWELVE BURSTS, NOT SIX: 48 tiles of SIXTEEN bytes. The shadow is indexed
14247               	; 	' by the same offset the PPU address uses, so it grows with the stride --
14248               	; 	' half of what it holds is the second bitplane, which this port never sets
14249               	; 	' and scan_or1 therefore never reads as ink.
14250               	; 	' AND THE CANVAS IS WIPED TO GREEN, NOT TO BLACK.
14251               	; 	'
14252               	; 	' On the TI a blank canvas is zeros and the COLOUR TABLE says what the
14253               	; 	' background is. There is no colour table here: a pixel's colour is its
14254               	; 	' two bitplane bits, so "green background" means plane 0 SET everywhere
14255               	; 	' and plane 1 clear -- index 1, which is the store's green in P0.
14256               	; 	'
14257               	; 	' THAT INVERTS THE SENSE OF EVERY FEATURE DRAWN ON TOP. The floor lines
14258               	; 	' add plane 1 to reach index 3 (gold), and the escalator diagonals CLEAR
14259               	; 	' plane 0 to reach index 0 (the backdrop, black) -- see scan_or1, which
14260               	; 	' is why it ANDs here and ORs on the TI. Writing zeros here instead would
14261               	; 	' leave the instrument black-on-black and the flights invisible.
14262               	; 	'
14263               	; 	' A tile is sixteen bytes: 0-7 are plane 0 and 8-15 plane 1, so the byte's
14264               	; 	' position within its tile decides which it is.
14265               	; 	' AND THE MARGINS ARE GREY, WHICH IS THE OTHER BITPLANE PAIR.
14266               	; 	'
14267               	; 	' The canvas is three character rows -- 24 pixel rows -- of which the
14268               	; 	' instrument uses the middle SIXTEEN (rows 4-19: four levels of four).
14269               	; 	' The outer eight are deliberate air, four above and four below, so the
14270               	; 	' radar does not butt against the shop floor above it or the screen edge
14271               	; 	' below. On the TI those rows take the scanner's own background; here they
14272               	; 	' are index 2, the store's grey, against the instrument's green.
14273               	; 	'
14274               	; 	' Two bitplanes give the four colours this canvas needs and nothing else
14275               	; 	' has to change: index 1 green is plane 0, index 2 grey is plane 1, and
14276               	; 	' the floor lines and flights work on top of those (scan_furn, scan_or1).
14277               	; 	'
14278               	; 	' The byte's place in the canvas says which it is. 256 bytes is one
14279               	; 	' CHARACTER row (16 tiles of 16), the low three bits are the pixel row
14280               	; 	' within the tile, and bit 3 of the position picks the bitplane.
14281               	; 	FOR swj = 0 TO 11
14282               	; 		FOR swi = 0 TO 63
14283               	; 			swv = #nsi AND 15		' 0-7 plane 0, 8-15 plane 1
14284               	; 			swr = #nsi AND 7		' pixel row inside the tile
14285               	; 			swc = #nsi / 256		' which character row, 0-2
14286               	; 			' NO MARGIN INSIDE THE CANVAS. All twenty-four pixel
14287               	; 			' rows are instrument now -- four bands of six -- and
14288               	; 			' the space around it is the grey strip drawn either
14289               	; 			' side in scan_canvas, which reaches the bottom of the
